what: The sections of this article, each with a line and a paragraph, for showing what the reader has already read. Built by admin/build/summaries.py from admin/content/articles/summaries/.

sections.label: The opening
sections.line: Brief people and agents from a self-maintaining knowledge graph
sections.para: The graph work is knowledge management: turn policies and internal information into a fractal semantic graph and brief from it, giving each reader the slice they need and the diff. Unlike vectors, a graph gives repeatable answers with paths. The graph need not be right, only maintained by agents, and sgit vaults carry the brief.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: A graph brief is an eighth of the text
sections.para: Policies become a graph with an ontology and taxonomy per element and named edges. The graphs of 112 articles hold 12.4% of their text, about 87,000 tokens against 704,000. Graphs give the same answer with its path, agents maintain them with a validator, odd edges prompt fixes, and briefs travel in sgit vaults.

sections.label: The idea
sections.line: Organisational knowledge should be a graph, not a pile
sections.para: Policies, standards, decisions and regulations usually reach people through a search box and documents. Instead, build a fractal semantic graph with each element in its owner's vocabulary and verbs that read both ways, such as owned_by, implemented_by and supersedes. Then brief from the part around a task and what changed.

sections.label: Briefing from the graph
sections.line: The site's article graphs hold 12.4% of the text
sections.para: The 112 articles carry 1,435 nodes and 1,538 edges. The text is about 704,000 tokens, the graphs as JSON about 199,000, and their words about 87,000: an eighth, with a median of 12.8%. Agents read graphs first and follow edges, and version diffs make what changed a list of nodes.

sections.label: Graphs and vectors
sections.line: Vectors find a starting point; graphs give reasons
sections.para: Embedding search helps when you do not know the organisation's words, but gives similarity, not a reason, and results move when the model or index changes. A graph walk over named edges gives the same answer each time, with its path. For policies, the path answering why we must do this is the answer.

sections.label: You do not have to get it right; you have to maintain it
sections.line: The graph need not be right, only maintained
sections.para: Projects that perfect the ontology first never ship. Agents propose nodes and edges and keep the rules, and code validates them. Asking why about odd edges yields fixes: 551 of 566 links pointed back in time, the control framework graph found six things the CSV omits, and the governance stack gained 119 edges.

sections.label: The brief has to travel
sections.line: sgit vaults deliver each brief only to its reader
sections.para: sgit encrypts files before they leave, so the server holds ciphertext, and every change is a commit. Scoped clones give an agent one folder, per-agent key pairs encrypt a brief to one reader, append lanes return findings without read access, and the vault's index says what to read now.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: Token counts are estimates and maintenance still needs owners
sections.para: Tokens were estimated as characters divided by four at v0.12.39. A graph helps choose what to read but does not replace reading, and vectors still help find starting points. The site's graphs compress well because of their contract, and someone must own the ontology at each altitude.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: Sources: a voice memo and this site's own graphs
sections.para: A voice memo of 14 October 2026 from a conversation about knowledge management, written up by this site's agent. The briefing figures were counted from the site's article markdown and graph files at v0.12.39, and the examples are the site's own articles and open vaults.
